content.text:
Claude Design doesn't have a direct "link a website URL" field, but here are the practical ways to reference the existing Hillsboro Village Dental homepage within that setup form:

**Best option: Screenshots as assets**
Take full-page screenshots of the homepage (sections: header, hero, features, footer, etc.) and upload them via **"Add fonts, logos and assets"**. Claude Design will visually analyze the current layout and design.

**Also helpful in "Any other notes":**
Paste the URL there (`https://www.hillsborovillagedental.com/`) along with a note like:
> "Reference this site for the current layout and content. Keep the structure but apply the new branding (fonts, colors, spacing) to match the assets provided."

Claude Design reads that field as context even if it can't live-browse the URL.

**If you have site code access:**
If the site's code is on GitHub or you can export it, the "Link code on GitHub" or "Link code from your computer" fields are the strongest signal — Claude can read the actual CSS/HTML to understand the current design system precisely.

**Recommended workflow for your case:**
1. Screenshot the full homepage (tools like GoFullPage Chrome extension work well)
2. Upload the screenshot(s) as assets alongside the logo files you already have
3. In "Any other notes", include the URL + the instruction to preserve layout/content but restyle with new branding
4. Describe the new brand direction (e.g., warm earthy tones, specific fonts if you know them)

The screenshot upload approach is the most reliable since Claude Design can directly see what needs to change.

For fastest sharing of a single HTML file, here are your best options ranked by speed:

**1. Netlify Drop (fastest, no account needed)**
Go to `app.netlify.com/drop`, drag the `.html` file in, and you get a live URL in seconds. Free, instant.

**2. Tiiny.host**
Upload the file at `tiiny.host`, get a shareable link immediately. Has a free tier with a simple link.

**3. surge.sh (CLI, ~30 seconds)**
If you have Node installed:
```bash
npx surge "/Users/richardvargas/Downloads/Bills Avenue Dental.html"
```
Gives you a `something.surge.sh` URL. Free.

**If this might become the permanent home:**
- **Netlify** — You already use Hostinger for LeftClick, but Netlify is great for static sites and you can keep the same URL if you upgrade and connect a custom domain later.

**My recommendation:** Netlify Drop. Zero setup, works in under a minute, and if the client wants it to stay live you can just create a free account and claim the site without re-uploading anything.

One thing to check first — does the HTML file reference any external CSS/JS/images, or is everything self-contained? If it has local asset dependencies, you'd need to zip those together before uploading.

For a single static HTML file — **Netlify wins easily**.

- **Netlify**: drag and drop, live in 30 seconds, free, built for static files
- **Railway**: built for apps with servers/databases, overkill for a static HTML file, and you'd need to configure a project

You already use Railway for the Basecamp proxy and email signature app (server-side apps) — that's the right use case for it. A static HTML mockup is exactly what Netlify Drop is made for.

For a static HTML file you're sharing with a client:

**Both are essentially equal**, but lean **Netlify** here because:

- Netlify Drop requires zero account — just drag and drop at `app.netlify.com/drop`
- Vercel requires signing in before you can deploy anything

If you were deploying a Next.js or React app, Vercel would be the stronger pick (it's made by the Next.js team). For a plain HTML file? Netlify is faster to get a link out.

name: claude-design-bundle-fix
description: Fix pattern for broken images in Claude Design-generated HTML bundles — relative paths vs window.__resources
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

When Claude Design generates a self-contained HTML file (using the `__bundler` system), all images are embedded in the `__bundler/manifest` as base64 data and mapped to named resource IDs in `__bundler/ext_resources`.

**The fix:** If an image shows as broken (displaying alt text instead of the photo), check the template for a relative file path like `uploads/filename.webp`. Change it to use the bundled resource:

```js
// Broken — relative path doesn't exist when hosted
photo: 'uploads/66788ab23426b24f74541344_dr-elizabeth.webp'

// Fixed — pulls from embedded bundle with fallback
photo: (window.__resources.drElizabeth || 'uploads/66788ab23426b24f74541344_dr-elizabeth.webp')
```

**Why:** Claude Design bundles assets by resource ID (e.g. `drElizabeth`, `teamKaren`). If the template hardcodes a relative path instead of referencing `window.__resources.resourceId`, the image only works locally — it breaks on any hosted URL.

**How to apply:** When a bundled HTML file has broken images after deploying to Netlify or any host, grep the template for `uploads/` or any relative image path and replace with the `window.__resources` pattern. The resource ID mapping is in the `__bundler/ext_resources` script tag.
